lesson.title: When the Past Goes Missing: Retrograde Amnesia
lesson.summary: Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before a brain injury or illness, the mirror image of anterograde amnesia's inability to form new ones.
lesson.body:
Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories that were formed before the onset of a brain injury, illness, or traumatic event. This makes it the mirror image of anterograde amnesia, which is the inability to form new long term memories after the onset of damage. A person with retrograde amnesia can often still learn new things going forward, but struggles to recall who they were, what they did, or what happened to them before the injury. A person with anterograde amnesia has the opposite problem: their past remains largely intact, but new experiences fail to become lasting memories. Some patients, including the famous case of Henry Molaison, known for decades in the research literature as H.M., show both patterns together after damage to the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures, though in H.M.'s case the anterograde deficit was far more severe and complete than his retrograde loss.

The hippocampus, discussed in the previous chapter, helps explain why retrograde amnesia happens at all. According to the standard model of memory consolidation, new experiences are not stored as finished, permanent memories the moment they occur. Instead, the hippocampus acts as a temporary hub that gradually helps stabilize a memory into more durable networks in the cerebral cortex, a process that can unfold over months or even years. When the hippocampus is damaged, memories still in this fragile, in progress stage of consolidation are especially vulnerable to being lost, while memories that finished consolidating long ago and now live mostly in cortical storage are more likely to survive.

This produces a well documented pattern sometimes called a temporal gradient, referred to by the nineteenth century term Ribot's Law: memories from just before the injury tend to be the most severely affected, while more distant childhood or early adulthood memories are often relatively preserved. A concussion offers an everyday, low stakes example of this same principle. An athlete who takes a hard hit to the head in a game may afterward be unable to recall the play that led to the injury, or even the last several minutes before it, while memories from earlier that day or from years before remain completely intact.

Retrograde amnesia can result from many causes beyond hippocampal injury, including traumatic brain injury, stroke, certain forms of dementia, and, temporarily, electroconvulsive therapy, which is sometimes associated with short term memory loss for events around the time of treatment. The length and severity of the memory loss generally scales with the severity of the underlying damage: a mild concussion might erase only a few minutes, while severe trauma or extensive hippocampal damage can erase years.

It is worth being cautious about overstating how neatly this maps onto every case, since amnesia in the real world is often messier than a textbook diagram suggests. Some patients recover portions of lost memory over time as swelling subsides or as cues help retrieval, while others never do. What stays consistent across cases, though, is the core distinction: retrograde amnesia is about the past disappearing, while anterograde amnesia is about the present failing to become a lasting past.
